title: Commutator decomposition for semisimple conjugation on a commutative unipotent group
statement: Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure]. Groups are affine group schemes [def-sc-group-scheme] of finite type over $k$ [def-weil-finite-type-morphism], and subgroups are closed subgroup schemes [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup]. Smoothness and connectedness mean [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms, def-weil-connected-scheme]. A point $s\in H(k)$ is semisimple if its image under every finite-dimensional algebraic representation $H\to\operatorname{GL}(V)$ is diagonalizable; an algebraic representation is a homomorphism of group schemes, $V$ is a finite-dimensional $k$-vector space, and $\operatorname{GL}(V)(A)$ is the group of invertible $A$-linear maps on $V\otimes_k A$. Let $H$ be smooth and connected and $N\subseteq H$ a smooth connected commutative normal subgroup which is unipotent: there is a closed immersion $N\hookrightarrow U_m$ for some $m\geq1$, where $U_m(A)$ consists of upper triangular $m\times m$ matrices with diagonal entries $1$ for each commutative $k$-algebra $A$. Let $s\in H(k)$ be semisimple. Define the centralizer $K=C_N(s)$ by $K(A)=\{n\in N(A):s_A n=n s_A\}$; it is the closed subscheme equalizing conjugation by $s$ and the identity on $N$ [def-weil-closed-immersion, def-pc-fibre-product]. Then $K$ is connected. Moreover, for every $x\in N(k)$ there exist $u\in N(k)$ and $v\in K(k)$ such that $x=[s,u]v$, where $[s,u]=sus^{-1}u^{-1}$.

source.place: Lemma 16.39, printed p.338. The rational-point decomposition is the rational-point consequence of its surjective morphism $N	imes C_N(s)	o N$ over an algebraically closed field.

proof.text: Put $a(n)=sns^{-1}$ and $c(n)=a(n)n^{-1}$. Normality of $N$ makes $a$ an automorphism of $N$. For every $k$-algebra $A$ and $n_1,n_2\in N(A)$, commutativity gives $c(n_1n_2)=a(n_1)a(n_2)n_2^{-1}n_1^{-1}=c(n_1)c(n_2)$. Thus $c:N\to N$ is a group-scheme homomorphism, and its scheme-theoretic kernel is exactly $K$. Apply [lem-sfb-algebraic-group-homomorphism-factorization] to write $c=j\circ q$, where $q:N\to M$ is faithfully flat and finitely presented and $j:M\hookrightarrow N$ is a closed immersion. All groups are affine and finite type, and hence separated, as required by that node. By [lem-sfb-group-hom-dimension-kernel-image], $\dim N=\dim M+\dim K$.

source.place: Lemma 16.39, printed p.338: commutator homomorphism, image and equation (121)

proof.text: We will lift rational points along $q$. Every fibre over $y\in M(k)$ is a nonempty affine finite-type $k$-scheme, since $q$ is surjective and is a morphism between affine finite-type schemes. Its coordinate algebra $B\ne0$ has a maximal ideal. Apply [lem-sfb-cardinal-generator-nullstellensatz] to a finite algebra-generating set of $B$: the cardinal bound holds because an algebraically closed field is infinite. The residue field is algebraic over $k$, hence equals $k$: the minimal polynomial of each algebraic element splits into linear factors over $k$, so that element belongs to $k$. This supplies a point of the fibre over $k$. The same argument applies below to fibres of any surjective homomorphism between the affine finite-type groups under consideration.

source.place: Lemma 16.39, printed p.338: lifting the point in the commutator image; the same elementary fibre argument will give the final rational-point conclusion

proof.text: Let $x\in(M\cap K)(k)$ and choose $u\in N(k)$ with $x=c(u)$ by step 2. The equality $x=sus^{-1}u^{-1}$ gives $x^{-1}s=usu^{-1}$, and $x$ commutes with $s$. Obtain a faithful finite-dimensional representation $\rho:H\hookrightarrow\operatorname{GL}(V)$ from [lem-sfb-central-torus-faithful-weight-blocks], with the central torus $T=1=\mathbf G_m^0$. Restrict $\rho$ to $N$. The stipulated immersion $N\hookrightarrow U_m\hookrightarrow\operatorname{GL}_m$ is faithful and sends $x$ to a unipotent matrix: its difference from the identity is strictly upper triangular, whose $m$th power is zero. Therefore [lem-sfb-rational-representation-unipotent-point], applied to $N$ and these two representations, makes $X=\rho(x)$ unipotent. Also $X^{-1}$ is unipotent, since $X^{-1}-1=-X^{-1}(X-1)$ and the two factors commute. Set $S=\rho(s)$, which is diagonalizable by the hypothesis on $s$. The commuting product $X^{-1}S=\rho(u)S\rho(u)^{-1}$ is itself diagonalizable, by conjugating an eigenbasis of $S$. It therefore has decompositions $(S,X^{-1})$ and $(X^{-1}S,1)$ into commuting diagonalizable and unipotent factors. Uniqueness in [lem-sfb-multiplicative-jordan-linear-compatibility] forces $X^{-1}=1$. Faithfulness of $\rho$ gives $x=1$. Thus $(M\cap K)(k)=\{1\}$.

source.place: Lemma 16.39, printed p.338: intersection with the centralizer and uniqueness of the Jordan decomposition

proof.text: The multiplication morphism $\mu:M\times_kK\to N$ is a homomorphism because $N$ is commutative. Its kernel $D$ is isomorphic as a group scheme to $M\cap K$: on every $k$-algebra the mutually inverse maps are $z\mapsto(z,z^{-1})$ and $(m,v)\mapsto m$, since $mv=1$ is equivalent to $v=m^{-1}$. Consequently $D(k)=\{1\}$ by step 3. Write $D=\operatorname{Spec}B$ with $B$ a nonzero finite-type $k$-algebra. By [lem-sfb-cardinal-generator-nullstellensatz], every maximal ideal has residue field $k$ by the argument of step 2, hence defines a $k$-point; there is therefore just one maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$. The same cited node says that every prime is the intersection of maximal ideals containing it; that intersection is now $\mathfrak m$. Thus $\operatorname{Spec}B$ consists of exactly one point. It follows directly that $D$ is connected and $\dim D=0$. This argument allows nilpotents in $B$; it does not assert that the kernel scheme is trivial or smooth.

source.place: Lemma 16.39, printed p.338: scheme-theoretic kernel of multiplication: connectedness and dimension zero, retaining possible infinitesimal structure

proof.text: By [lem-sfb-scheme-product-dimension], $\dim(M\times_kK)=\dim M+\dim K$ for the dimension of [def-pc-dimension]; both factors are nonempty because they are group schemes. By [lem-pc-scheme-dimension-local-rings] this dimension equals the topological Krull dimension used in [lem-sfb-group-hom-dimension-kernel-image], for $M\times_kK$, $M$ and $K$ alike, so step 1 gives $\dim(M\times_kK)=\dim N$ topologically. The kernel of $\mu$ has dimension zero by step 4, and the target $N$ is smooth and connected by hypothesis. The surjectivity criterion in [lem-sfb-group-hom-dimension-kernel-image] therefore says that $\mu$ is faithfully flat. Apply [lem-sfb-connected-group-extension] to $\mu$, whose connected kernel is $D$ and whose connected target is $N$. It follows that $M\times_kK$ is connected. Its projection onto $K$ is a continuous surjection, since it has the section $v\mapsto(1,v)$, so $K$ is connected. No smoothness of $D$ is needed.

source.place: Lemma 16.39, printed p.338: surjectivity of multiplication and connectedness by Proposition 5.59

proof.text: For $x\in N(k)$ the surjectivity of $\mu$ gives a nonempty affine finite-type fibre. Apply [lem-sfb-cardinal-generator-nullstellensatz] exactly as in step 2 to find $(m,v)\in M(k)\times K(k)$ in that fibre; thus $x=mv$. Step 2 applied to $q$ gives $u\in N(k)$ with $c(u)=m$. Consequently $x=[s,u]v$, which is the required decomposition.
